2021_218_8_b_24680_troy_school_district_.paragraph: Plante & Moran, PLLC's Report to the Board of Education for Troy School District covers the audit of the basic financial statements for the year ended June 30, 2021, dated October 5, 2021 and signed by partner Donna Hanson, CPA and manager Michael Walsh, CPA. It pairs required auditor communications with informational items on state and federal funding, MPSERS, fund balance, and coming accounting standards, reporting no disagreements with management and no new accounting policies. **Item and Source**
Agenda item 8.B., meeting of October 19, 2021. "Troy School District — Report to the Board of Education, June 30, 2021," prepared by Plante & Moran, PLLC. Report letters are dated October 5, 2021. Signed by Donna Hanson, CPA (Partner) and Michael Walsh, CPA (Manager). The firm thanks Mr. Rick West, Ms. Kandice Moynihan, and the business office. Contents: Results of the Audit, pages 1-4; Informational Items, pages 5-15.

**Required Auditor Communications**
The engagement letter is dated June 2, 2021; the audit followed the scope and timing set at the planning meeting of August 13, 2021, under U.S. GAAS and Government Auditing Standards, with a separate internal control and compliance letter and a 2 CFR Part 200 single audit report both dated October 5, 2021. No new accounting policies were adopted and none changed during 2021. There were no transactions lacking authoritative guidance, no significant difficulties or disagreements with management, and no consultations with other independent accountants. Management corrected all immaterial misstatements and signed a representation letter dated October 5, 2021.

**Most Sensitive Estimates**
The District's share of MPSERS net liabilities under GASB Statements Nos. 68 and 75, based on data from the Office of Retirement Services:

| Estimate at June 30, 2021 | Amount |
| --- | --- |
| Net pension liability | $308,094,061 |
| Net OPEB liability | $48,088,931 |

**State Aid Background**
The May 2020 Revenue Estimating Conference suggested proration estimated at $685 per pupil; the August 2020 conference produced an actual proration of $175 per pupil for 2019-2020. For 2020-2021 the foundation allowance was held at 2019-2020 levels with a $65 one-time per pupil payment. The 2020-2021 target foundation allowance was $8,529 and the minimum foundation allowance remained $8,111. A one-year "super blend" pupil count weighted the 2019-2020 count at 75 percent and the 2020-2021 count at 25 percent. For 2021-2022 all districts move to a target foundation of $8,700 per pupil with at least a $171 per pupil increase; for hold harmless districts such as Troy, that $171 arrives as $115 of foundation allowance and $56 of Section 20m funding. Pupil counts return to 90 percent fall / 10 percent spring weighting.

**MPSERS and Federal Funding**
The estimated 2020-2021 MPSERS contribution rate ranged from 35.47 to 42.72 percent of payroll, and from 20.96 to 28.21 percent net of state support. District receipts were $1,070,809 in Section 147a1, $1,838,621 in 147a2, $11,658,202 in 147c1, and $206,687 in 147e. For 2022 the overall rate is expected to rise to 43 percent from 42 percent, with net cost approximating 28 percent. Coronavirus Relief Fund distributions of approximately $362 per pupil totaled $4,588,959 for the District and were fully expended in the year ended June 30, 2021. ESSER I was awarded at $246,411, with ESSER II and III estimated at $843,258 and $1,893,840. Against the $450 per pupil ESSER II floor, the District qualified for a state equalization payment of $5,036,199 received across the May through August 2021 state aid payments, recognized partly in fiscal 2021 with the remainder in fiscal 2022. A $1,093 per student floor was set for ESSER III, though its legality was being questioned federally.

**Fund Balance**
General Fund revenue exceeded expenditures by approximately $6,700,000 in 2020-2021, raising General Fund fund balance to approximately $32,700,000 at June 30, 2021. The District's fund balance percentage is 19.88 percent, about 10.3 weeks of operation; the statewide average at June 30, 2020 was approximately 15.90 percent, roughly 8 weeks.

**Upcoming Standards and Advisory Topics**
GASB Statement No. 87 (Leases) and SAS No. 134, issued May 2019, both take effect for June 30, 2022. The GASB financial reporting model project, begun August 2013 with a June 2020 exposure draft and comment period ending February 2021, targets final standards by June 2022, with phased adoption at June 30, 2025 for districts over $75 million in revenue and June 30, 2026 below. Also covered: grants management risk, budgeting, the proposed "Enhancing K-12 Cybersecurity Act" ($10 million yearly for two years), and an optional IT assessment.
2021_218_8_b_24680_troy_school_district_.verbose:
Agenda item 8.B. for the Troy School District Board of Education meeting of October 19, 2021 is the annual "Report to the Board of Education" for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2021, prepared by the District's independent auditors, Plante & Moran, PLLC. The transmittal letter and all component letters are dated October 5, 2021. The report is signed by Donna Hanson, CPA, Partner, and Michael Walsh, CPA, Manager. The firm records its thanks to Mr. Rick West, Ms. Kandice Moynihan, and the entire business office for assistance and preparedness during the audit, noting that audit preparation is carried out in addition to staff's normal daily activities. The document is organized in two parts: Results of the Audit at pages 1-4 and Informational Items at pages 5-15.

RESULTS OF THE AUDIT. Plante & Moran audited the financial statements of Troy School District as of and for the year ended June 30, 2021 and issued its report thereon dated October 5, 2021. The engagement letter is dated June 2, 2021; internal control was considered solely to determine audit procedures. The audit was also conducted under Government Auditing Standards issued by the Comptroller General of the United States, with a separate letter dated October 5, 2021 covering internal control over financial reporting and compliance testing. Scope and timing followed the planning meeting of August 13, 2021.

Significant audit findings: significant accounting policies are described in Note 2. No new accounting policies were adopted and the application of existing policies was not changed during 2021. No transactions lacked authoritative guidance or consensus, and none were recognized in a period different from when they occurred. The most sensitive estimates were the District's share of the MPSERS net liabilities for the pension and other postemployment benefit (OPEB) plans recorded on the government-wide statements under GASB Statement Nos. 68 and 75; the District's estimates as of June 30, 2021 were $308,094,061 for the pension plan and $48,088,931 for the OPEB plan, based on data from the Office of Retirement Services. Disclosures are described as neutral, consistent, and clear. There were no significant difficulties with management, no disagreements, and no consultations with other independent accountants; management corrected all immaterial misstatements and signed a representation letter dated October 5, 2021. A 2 CFR Part 200 audit of federal programs was completed, with the compliance report dated October 5, 2021. The auditors read the Annual Comprehensive Financial Report and noted nothing materially inconsistent.

STATE AID FUNDING BACKGROUND. Spring 2020 predictions of negative impacts to the School Aid Fund led to two Revenue Estimating Conferences, the scheduled one in May 2020 and an additional conference in August 2020. The May conference suggested proration estimated at $685 per pupil, and many districts adopted a final 2020 budget amendment reflecting it; by August 2020 the result was a proration of $175 per pupil for the 2019-2020 fiscal year. Federal assistance began in March 2020 and arrived in waves through 2020 and 2021. For 2020-2021 the foundation allowance was held at the 2019-2020 level, no prorations were required, and a $65 one-time per pupil payment was provided; the State also funded districts that fell below a minimum per pupil threshold from the new Educational Stabilization Fund federal program. For 2021-2022, all schools reach the target foundation allowance of $8,700 per pupil, eliminating the equity gap between base and target foundations, with all schools including hold harmless districts receiving at least a $171 per pupil increase, plus progress on School Finance Research Collaborative recommendations covering special education, At-Risk, wraparound services such as nurses and counselors, and Great Start Readiness (GSRP).

2021 FUNDING IMPLICATIONS FOR THE DISTRICT. The 2020-2021 target foundation allowance (formerly the basic foundation allowance) was $8,529 and the minimum foundation allowance remained $8,111; the District received a one-time per pupil payment of $65 that was not added to the foundation formula and not retained for 2021-2022. A one-year "super blend" pupil count combined the 2019-2020 count weighted at 75 percent with the 2020-2021 count weighted at 25 percent.

MPSERS COST SUPPORT. Contributions are computed as a percentage of payroll and the required rate continues to increase. The estimated contribution rate for 2020-2021 ranged from 35.47 to 42.72 percent, with the rate net of state funding support, paid directly by the employer, ranging from 20.96 to 28.21 percent. State support flows through Sections 147a, 147c, and 147e of the State Aid Act. The District received $1,070,809 in 147a1, $1,838,621 in 147a2, $11,658,202 in 147c1, and $206,687 of 147e. The total cost of retirement contributions in 2020-2021 represents approximately 42 percent of covered payroll recognized as expenditure, with the District responsible for approximately a 28 percent contribution net of state support.

CORONAVIRUS RELIEF FUND. In summer 2020, approximately $362 per pupil was provided to districts by the Michigan Department of Education through summer state aid payments; the total available to Troy School District was $4,588,959. Because the funding was not approved until July 2020, revenue recognition was deferred to fiscal year 2021, and for the year ended June 30, 2021 the District fully expended the award and recognized the related federal revenue.

PANDEMIC-RELATED FEDERAL FUNDING AND ESSER. Key sources are the Education Stabilization Fund (ESF), whose principal programs are the Elementary and Secondary School Emergency Relief (ESSER) Fund and the Governor's Education Emergency Relief (GEER) Fund, and the Coronavirus Relief Fund. Reimbursement claims could reach back to March 2020. ESSER grants come in three waves: ESSER I, ESSER II (phases 1 and 2), and ESSER III. The District's ESSER I award was $246,411, with ESSER II and ESSER III estimates of $843,258 and $1,893,840. Many districts did not receive phase 1 ESSER II award letters by June 30, 2021, deferring that revenue to fiscal 2022; phase 2 of ESSER II and ESSER III awards become available in fiscal year 2022. ESSER allocations follow the Title I model using economically disadvantaged demographics, so the Legislature and governor set a per pupil floor of $450 for ESSER II; based on its ESSER II level, the District qualified for an equalization payment of $5,036,199 received over the May through August 2021 state aid payments, recognized partly as fiscal 2021 revenue with the remainder in fiscal 2022.

2022 FUNDING IMPLICATIONS. The May 2021 Revenue Estimating Conference was optimistic for 2022, 2023, and 2024. Districts not at the target level in 2021 move to the new $8,700 per pupil target; those already at or above the former $8,529 target receive the $171 per pupil increase. For hold harmless districts such as Troy, the $171 increase is expected in two pieces: $115 per pupil of foundation allowance and $56 per pupil of Section 20m funding. The State set an ESSER III funding floor of $1,093 per student, but the federal government has begun questioning its legality. Pupil membership returns to the pre-fiscal year 2021 method for 2021-2022, weighted 90 percent fall and 10 percent spring. Resources went to summer 2021 programming, credit recovery, and before- and after-school programming through ESSER II plus state appropriations. For 2021-2022 the overall MPSERS contribution rate is expected to increase to 43 percent from 42 percent, with net cost to the District approximating 28 percent.

LOOKING FORWARD TO 2023 AND BEYOND. 2021 carries a projected surplus into 2022, with surpluses expected for 2023 and 2024. Monitoring factors include the economic "bounce back," tapering federal stimulus, the return to in-class instruction, learning loss, enrollment changes, personnel shortages, staffing costs, and retirement system cost trends. The next Revenue Estimating Conference will occur in January 2022.

GRANTS MANAGEMENT AND BUDGETING. The report catalogs increased grants management burden across leadership, board members, the business office, staff, procurement, information technology, support services, and facilities, and recommends a fiscal 2022 risk assessment of key processes and controls. Budget guidance covers multiyear revenue forecasting, monitoring pupil counts, separating recurring contractual payroll from variable pandemic-funded payroll, and budgeting one-time uses of assistance. Federal grant program end dates are laddered through 2024.

MPSERS PLAN STATUS. The MPSERS plan has a September 30 year end. At September 30, 2020 the pension portion had a net pension liability of approximately $35 billion, an increase from $33.8 billion at September 30, 2019, an increase of approximately 3.5 percent, driven largely by less than favorable actuarial experience. At September 30, 2020 the retiree health care (OPEB) portion had a net OPEB liability of approximately $5.4 billion, a decrease from $7.3 billion at September 30, 2019, a decrease of approximately 26 percent, reflecting a reduction in the health care cost trend rate from 7.5 percent to 7.0 percent and favorable plan experience from lower than projected health benefit costs.

FUND BALANCE. During the 2020-2021 school year the District's General Fund revenue exceeded expenditures by approximately $6,700,000, increasing General Fund fund balance to approximately $32,700,000 at June 30, 2021. The statewide average for school districts at June 30, 2020 was approximately 15.90 percent of expenditures, roughly equal to average operating costs for an 8-week period. The District's fund balance percentage is 19.88 percent, equal to approximately 10.3 weeks of operation. The report cautions that Consumer Price Index growth and decisions on spending COVID-19 relief funds will pressure fund balance in 2021-2022.

CYBERSECURITY AND IT. Education remains a top ransomware target. The "Enhancing K-12 Cybersecurity Act," introduced in the House in June 2021, would appropriate $10 million yearly for two years for a school cybersecurity program. The auditors note weak passwords such as "August2021," raise questions about PII and FERPA-covered data on file-sharing sites, flash drives, and personal email, and offer an external vulnerability assessment plus a broader IT assessment covering governance, IT staffing, external service providers, service delivery, network and device management, and cybersecurity policies.

ACCOUNTING AND AUDITING CHANGES. GASB Statement No. 87 (Leases) is effective for the District's June 30, 2022 financial statements, requiring lessees to recognize a lease liability and intangible right-of-use asset and lessors a lease receivable and deferred inflow of resources, with an inventory of lease and embedded-lease contracts needed. SAS No. 134, "Auditor Reporting and Amendments, including Amendments Addressing Disclosures in the Audit of Financial Statements," issued by the AICPA Auditing Standards Board in May 2019, takes effect for the June 30, 2022 audited financial statements, moving the opinion to the top of the letter, expanding the basis of opinion section, explaining materiality and reasonable assurance, enhancing going concern reporting, and introducing key audit matters. The GASB financial reporting model project began in August 2013; an exposure draft titled "Financial Reporting Model Improvements" was issued in June 2020 with a comment period ending February 2021 on which Plante & Moran commented, and the GASB goal is final standards by June 2022. Proposed changes include more MD&A information, a budget-to-actual column showing variances between original and amended budget, renaming "revenue" as "inflows of resources" and "expenditures" as "outflows of resources," and replacing modified accrual with a "short-term financial resources measurement focus" covering amounts converted to or paid in cash within 12 months of year end, versus today's 60-day receivable rule. Phased adoption would apply at June 30, 2025 for districts with total annual revenue across all funds over $75 million and June 30, 2026 for those under $75 million. A related GASB preliminary views document, "Revenue and Expense Recognition," was released in June 2020, with a standard anticipated during 2025.
